newsitem.title: USA: Defense entitled to research data in smoke trial.
newsitem.headline: Defense entitled to research data in smoke trial.

text.p: A Florida judge said on Monday the defense in an upcoming class-action lawsuit against the tobacco industry should have access to the raw data used in scientific reports on the effects of passive smoking.
"We are entitled to have our experts review that data," Hugh Whiting, attorney for defendant RJ Reynolds Tobacco, a unit of RJR Nabisco, told a pre-trail hearing before Judge Robert Kaye.

It is filed on behalf of an estimated 60,000 non-smoking flight attentants suffering from lung diseases and other ailments allegedly caused by second-hand smoke on U.S. passenger jets. Trial is due to begin on June 2.

Judge Kaye also heard arguments over the proposed plan for the trial. The tobacco industry wants the jury initially to consider whether second-hand smoke causes disease and later the industry's liability. The plaintiffs do not want the two issues separated.
"We are saying this doesn't need to be proved. The tobacco companies, with all their resources, are questioning every finding. We can't bring in 2,000 scientists," Rosenblatt said.
Defense attorney David Ross called her remarks "outrageous" and said the plaintiffs, having brought the case, were now trying to avoid having to prove it.
"If they can't prove this then we go home," he said.
Kaye said it was not accepted that second-hand smoke caused cancer but he did not issue a formal ruling on the motion.
He also declined to impose a gag order on plaintiff's attorney Stanley Rosenblatt but he said he did not want lawyers discussing the merits of the case with the media.
"I'm not going to gag the media but attorneys should be more circumsepct in what they say," he said.
Philip Morris attorney David Hardy said Mr. Rosenblatt had been regularly utilizing the media to prejudice members of the public, including potential jurors.

Hardy said Rosenblatt acted improperly by leaking to the Miami Herarld the transcript of depositions taken from tobacco industry chief executives. Rosenblatt also showed excerpts from those depositions on the CBS television show "60 Minutes" on Sunday night.
Rosenblatt contended that media interest in the tobacco industry was intense and had nothing to do with his involvement.

Attorneys for three newspapers -- the Wall Street Journal, Miami Herald and USA Today -- asked the court not to impose the gag order. "It would be a complete violation of the First Amendment to the Constitution," Dan Paul, attorney for Dow Jones & Co, which owns the Journal, told the court.
